overview: This file documents U.S.–Japanese arrangements for reciprocal recognition of vessel-tonnage and admeasurement certificates. It combines a 1933 Japanese diplomatic note announcing revisions to Japan’s ship-measurement law with English translations of the revised law, detailed measurement regulations, and simplified rules for vessels under twenty metres, followed by a 1937 exchange concerning amendments governing shelter-deck drainage and the measurement of water-ballast tanks. Department of State and Department of Commerce correspondence shows the amendments being reviewed against American rules, accepted as substantially equivalent, and communicated back to Japan, with British practice also cited as an influence.

subfiles.title: Japanese note on the revised ship-measurement law
subfiles.about: The Japanese Ambassador reports changes to Japan’s ship-measurement law and requests continued reciprocal recognition of measurement certificates.
subfiles.summary: The note explains that Law No. 34 of 1914 was amended by Law No. 6 of 1931 and that the amendment took effect on June 20, 1932. The principal changes replace “register tonnage” with “net tonnage,” standardize the tonnage unit, and simplify measurement of ships under twenty metres. Because older rules temporarily remained applicable to vessels not yet remeasured, two classes of Japanese measurement certificates were expected to coexist until approximately September 30, 1934.

subfiles.title: Referral of the Japanese note to the Department of Commerce
subfiles.about: The State Department forwards the Japanese note and translated measurement rules to the Department of Commerce for consideration.
subfiles.summary: The Secretary of State transmits a copy of Japanese Embassy note No. 70 and its enclosure. Commerce is asked to consider Japan’s amendments and its request to continue bilateral recognition of ship-measurement certificates.

subfiles.title: Acknowledgment of Japanese note No. 70
subfiles.about: The State Department acknowledges Japan’s notification and says that the matter has been referred to the appropriate U.S. authorities.
subfiles.summary: The Secretary of State thanks the Ambassador for note No. 70 concerning amendments to Japanese ship-measurement law. He promises a further communication after receiving a response from the responsible American authorities.

subfiles.title: English translation of the Ship Measurement Law
subfiles.about: This enclosure gives the amended Japanese statutory framework for calculating the gross and net tonnage of ships.
subfiles.summary: The law defines the tonnage deck, gross capacity, net capacity, allowable deductions, machinery-space calculations, and special treatment of ships under twenty metres. Its supplementary provisions govern the transition from older measurement rules, remeasurement, taxation, registration, subsidies, and vessels previously measured in koku. The 1931 amendments substitute “net tonnage” for “net register tonnage” and preserve certain existing registrations and pledges.

subfiles.title: English translation of the Ship Measurement Regulations
subfiles.from: Japanese Department of State for Communications
subfiles.about: These regulations prescribe detailed surveying and mathematical procedures for measuring vessels twenty metres or more in length.
subfiles.summary: The regulations define the length, breadth, depth, tonnage deck, shelter deck, and measurement points used to calculate hull volume. They provide formulas for capacity below and above the tonnage deck, exemptions from gross capacity, and deductions used to derive net capacity, including crew spaces, ballast tanks, machinery spaces, boatswain’s stores, and navigational or safety equipment. Special provisions address open ships, dredgers, complex hull forms, passenger spaces, hatchways, shelter-deck openings, and unusual construction.

subfiles.title: Simplified Measurement Regulations for Ships
subfiles.from: Japanese Department of State for Communications
subfiles.about: This enclosure establishes simplified tonnage calculations for ships under twenty metres in length.
subfiles.summary: The rules define ship length, breadth, and depth and prescribe simplified coefficients for calculating the capacity of steel and wooden vessels. They specify exclusions for certain deck structures and establish standard deductions for vessels with and without propulsion machinery. Supplementary provisions bring the rules into force with the 1931 amendment and allow pending applications to be handled under the earlier regulations; the Japanese colophon records printing on June 23, 1932.

subfiles.title: Japanese note No. 27 on amendments to Articles 21 and 29
subfiles.about: Japan reports two technical amendments to its vessel-tonnage regulations and asks that reciprocal recognition of certificates continue.
subfiles.summary: The note transmits the substance of Ordinance No. 51 of October 13, 1936. Article 21 replaces freeing ports and smaller scuppers near a shelter-deck opening with accessible automatic screw-down non-return valves at least thirteen centimetres in diameter; Article 29 revises the division of water-ballast-tank lengths for measurement. Japan states that the first change follows British practice and that the second largely preserves the earlier rule while altering the calculation method.

subfiles.title: Referral of Japanese note No. 27 to Commerce
subfiles.about: The State Department forwards Japan’s 1937 amendments and renewed request for reciprocal recognition to the Department of Commerce.
subfiles.summary: The note encloses Japanese Embassy note No. 27 for Commerce Department review. It identifies the amended provisions as Articles 21 and 29 of Japan’s vessel-tonnage regulations and highlights Japan’s request that recognition of its certificates continue.

subfiles.title: Acknowledgment of Japanese note No. 27
subfiles.about: The State Department acknowledges the 1937 Japanese amendments and confirms their referral to the appropriate U.S. authorities.
subfiles.summary: The Secretary of State thanks the Ambassador for note No. 27 concerning amendments to Articles 21 and 29. The reply states that the matter has been sent to the responsible authorities of the United States Government.

subfiles.title: Commerce recommendation on Japanese admeasurement amendments
subfiles.about: The Commerce Department finds the Japanese amendments compatible with American rules and recommends continued recognition of Japanese certificates.
subfiles.summary: Commerce reviews the new shelter-deck valve requirement and the revised method for dividing water-ballast tanks between nine and fifteen metres in length. It concludes that both provisions are practically in accord with United States admeasurement rules and recommends continued reciprocity. Two copies of Circular Letter No. 124 concerning tonnage openings and shelter-deck scupperage are supplied for the Japanese Government.

subfiles.title: United States concurrence in continued reciprocal recognition
subfiles.about: The United States formally accepts the amended Japanese rules as substantially equivalent to its own and continues reciprocal recognition of certificates.
subfiles.summary: The reply restates the amendments concerning automatic non-return valves and the four-part division of water-ballast tanks between nine and fifteen metres. Because the revised Japanese regulations remain substantially in accord with American rules, the United States agrees to continue recognition of Japanese admeasurement certificates. Two copies of Commerce Department Circular Letter No. 124 are enclosed for information.

subfiles.title: Japanese acknowledgment of Circular Letter No. 124
subfiles.about: The Japanese Ambassador acknowledges the American reply and confirms that the Commerce circular will be sent to the responsible Japanese department.
subfiles.summary: Japanese Embassy note No. 72 thanks the Secretary of State for his March 12 communication and the two copies of Circular Letter No. 124. It reports that arrangements have been made to forward the circular to the competent department of the Japanese Government.

interest: The file is particularly useful because it preserves not merely the diplomatic decision to recognize Japanese tonnage certificates, but extensive English translations of the underlying Japanese law and its highly technical implementing rules. It reveals how regulatory equivalence was negotiated through detailed comparisons of valves, scuppers, shelter-deck openings, ballast tanks, and measurement formulas, while also showing British influence on Japanese practice. The combination of legal texts, technical standards, diplomatic notes, and interdepartmental correspondence offers a compact case study of international maritime standardization and routine U.S.–Japanese administrative cooperation during the 1930s.
